image_prompt.text: Open, relatively sheltered ground around the starting shelter with room to grow outward into connected rooms, a garage, a greenhouse, a workshop and a lookout tower
Shelters and abandoned structures players actually go inside — the player's own base rooms, research stations, the crashed aircraft and shipwrecks
The cold itself as the threat: exposed open ice where wind and blizzards strip warmth, with whiteouts sweeping across the landscape
Ice fields, glaciers, ridges and rugged mountains shaping the ground, with caves and ice tunnels cutting under it
Frozen lakes inland and open sea offshore where the orcas surface
Antarctic wildlife inhabiting the map — penguin colonies and seals on the coastal ice, birds overhead, orcas offshore — and no fantasy monsters anywhere
Points of interest scattered across the ice: abandoned research stations, crashed aircraft, shipwrecks, mouths of ice tunnels
Campfires and heaters as warm points in the landscape, the only relief from the cold outside the base

layout_placement.text: Gatherable resources graded by distance from base: driftwood, scrap metal, ice, stone, fabric, fuel, electronics, animal hides and food nearby, rare scientific equipment and blueprints far out
Journals and recordings left by the earlier expeditions, read where they are found

mechanics: Spawn with only basic survival supplies
Body temperature is the primary survival mechanic; warmth decreases outside and wind and storms speed it up
Campfires and heaters restore warmth
Hunger and energy exist but are secondary
Freezing slows movement before causing death
Return to shelter before storms or nightfall
Build walls, floors, roofs and foundations; place furniture and storage; install insulation, generators, heating, solar panels and wind turbines
Shelter upgrades reduce heating costs and protect from storms
Higher-tier resources require travelling farther from base
Unlock snowmobile, snowcat, cargo sled and a late-game helicopter
Dynamic weather: blizzards, whiteouts, high winds, extreme cold
Day/night cycle with auroras
Uncover the story through journals, recordings and environmental storytelling
Minimal UI focused on immersion
notes: world-biomes carries P4 in the catalogue and it is overridden to a single continuous build here, because the prompt asks explicitly for a large seamless open world. The biome variety stays; the map split does not.
P2 is required for the caves and ice tunnels, which the universal terrain note calls out as pushing terrain past tiered.

Extent and detail cannot both be honoured: a continent of ice framed in one render will not also show furniture inside a shelter. The base interior is the obvious candidate for a separate detailed pass if the user wants both.
Weather, the day/night cycle and the auroras have no home in this handoff and are recorded in mechanics for whoever owns the sky.

notes_for_us: This prompt has four separate whole-build rules — seamless world, semi-realistic, no fantasy monsters, and six named reference games — and constraints held all of them cleanly. It is the clearest case yet for that field existing; before it, 'avoid fantasy monsters' had nowhere to go but silence.

Weather and the day/night cycle are load-bearing for this game (temperature is the core mechanic) and the handoff has no sky field at all, so they land in mechanics where a layout reader will ignore them.

The extent-versus-detail conflict is real here and the skill tells me to offer the split, but open_questions is the only place to offer it, which makes an architectural decision look like one of four equal questions.

mechanics: You are given one character to start with

notes: This is the find-and-unlock family, so the map is one continuous searchable surface and routes P0.
The prompt names no setting at all — not a place, a period or a mood — so theme is null rather than guessed, and the map's subject is genuinely unresolved.
Character count is unstated and it drives the whole layout: a dozen hiding places and a hundred are different maps.
